arguments.title: Mom's 2028 Rx plan — neutral side-by-side (as of 9/5/27)
arguments.body:
MOM'S 2028 Rx PLAN — NEUTRAL SIDE-BY-SIDE
Prepared: 2027-09-05
For: Oct 17, 2027 11:00–11:30a Central review with Riley (evt_1789868252899)
Status: COMPARISON ONLY — no election, no recommendation, no enrollment

WHAT THIS IS
- A neutral, side-by-side comparison of two 2028 prescription-plan brochures.
- Premium, deductible, and known-medication copay math using only confirmed fields.
- A visible list of every formulary, pharmacy, and structural detail that must be
  verified before Oct 17 so the comparison can be completed and Mom can elect.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
- Not an enrollment decision. Mom retains election; no enrollment action taken.
- Not a recommendation of one plan over the other.
- Not a complete formulary comparison for either plan.
- Not a forecast of Mom's 2028 utilization or spend.
- Not a substitute for Mom's own review with the broker / 1-800-MEDICARE / SHIP.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PLAN A — KNOWN: Golden State Rx Saver 2028
------------------------------------------------------------------
Source: 2028 plan notice already in hand (the "known" plan).
Annual drug deductible:        $650
Monthly premium:                $38.20
Annual premium:                 $458.40  ($38.20 × 12)

Known covered medications (only these three are confirmed):
  - lisinopril 10 mg
      Preferred-pharmacy copay: $0
      Tier designation:         not stated in notice (marked to verify)
  - atorvastatin 20 mg
      Preferred-pharmacy copay: $0
      Tier designation:         not stated in notice (marked to verify)
  - Ventolin HFA 90 mcg/actuation
      Subject to deductible, then $52 preferred-pharmacy copay
      Tier designation:         not stated in notice (marked to verify)

Pharmacy network (confirmed):
  - River Park Community Pharmacy = in-network, preferred

------------------------------------------------------------------
PLAN B — UNNAMED COMPETING 2028 PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------
Source: first competing 2028 brochure, received 9/5/27. Plan name not yet in hand.
Annual drug deductible:        $590
Monthly premium:                $44.10
Annual premium:                 $529.20  ($44.10 × 12)

Known covered medications (only these three are confirmed):
  - lisinopril 10 mg
      Tier:                     1
      Preferred-pharmacy copay: $2
  - atorvastatin 20 mg
      Tier:                     1
      Preferred-pharmacy copay: $2
  - Ventolin HFA 90 mcg/actuation
      Subject to deductible, then $47 preferred-pharmacy copay
      Tier designation:         not stated in brochure (marked to verify)

Pharmacy network (confirmed):
  - River Park Community Pharmacy = in network
  - Preferred status under Plan B = NOT stated in brochure (marked to verify)

------------------------------------------------------------------
PREMIUM MATH (clean, no assumptions)
------------------------------------------------------------------
Annual premium, Plan A (Golden State Rx Saver):  $458.40
Annual premium, Plan B (unnamed competing):      $529.20
Annual premium difference:                        $70.80
                                                   Plan B is $70.80/year higher
                                                   (+15.4% vs Plan A)

------------------------------------------------------------------
DEDUCTIBLE MATH (clean, no assumptions)
------------------------------------------------------------------
Annual deductible, Plan A:  $650
Annual deductible, Plan B:  $590
Deductible difference:      $60
                             Plan B is $60/year lower
                             (−9.2% vs Plan A)

Premium + deductible headline (Plan B − Plan A):
  +$70.80 (premium) − $60.00 (deductible) = +$10.80 net higher per year on Plan B
  before any copay or utilization differences.

------------------------------------------------------------------
KNOWN-MEDICATION COPAY MATH (12 fills/year assumption — to verify)
------------------------------------------------------------------
Assumptions used (each is marked to verify):
  - 12 fills per medication per year (one per month, retail).
  - Tier 1 generic copays apply all 12 months without deductible application.
  - Ventolin HFA copays apply only after the annual deductible is met.
  - For Plan A Ventolin, the deductible is met by some fill; copay of $52
    applies on fills after that fill. (Plan B is identical structurally but $47.)
  - No mail-order is modeled — both brochures' mail-order terms are unverified.
  - No tier-2/3/4 or non-preferred-pharmacy pricing is modeled.
  - No coverage-gap (donut hole) or catastrophic-phase pricing is modeled —
    2028 thresholds not yet published and not in either brochure excerpt.

Plan A — Golden State Rx Saver — annual copay estimate (12 fills each):
  lisinopril 10 mg   12 × $0  =  $0
  atorvastatin 20 mg 12 × $0  =  $0
  Ventolin HFA       12 × $52 = $624  (post-deductible only; deductible met separately)
  Subtotal:                  $624

Plan B — unnamed competing — annual copay estimate (12 fills each):
  lisinopril 10 mg   12 × $2  = $24
  atorvastatin 20 mg 12 × $2  = $24
  Ventolin HFA       12 × $47 = $564  (post-deductible only; deductible met separately)
  Subtotal:                  $612

Copay difference on the three known meds, Plan B vs Plan A: −$12
(i.e., Plan B is $12/year cheaper in copays on these three meds, ignoring deductible
allocation and any tier-1 generic deductible exemption that may apply.)

------------------------------------------------------------------
HEADLINE TOTAL — premium + deductible + known-med copays
(12 fills/yr assumption; deductible met once per year by Ventolin alone)
------------------------------------------------------------------
Plan A: $458.40 + $650.00 + $624.00 = $1,732.40
Plan B: $529.20 + $590.00 + $612.00 = $1,731.20
Difference: Plan B is $1.20 lower than Plan A under this single scenario.

This headline is sensitive to assumptions marked below. It is not a recommendation.
If lisinopril/atorvastatin are deductible-exempt on Plan A (a common Part D feature),
Plan A's deductible is not reduced by their copays, and the headline widens in
Plan A's favor. That is one of the verification items.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SIDE-BY-SIDE — clean comparison, confirmed fields only
------------------------------------------------------------------
Field                            Plan A                Plan B
                                Golden State Rx       Unnamed competing
                                Saver 2028            (brochure 9/5/27)
Monthly premium                  $38.20                $44.10
Annual premium                   $458.40               $529.20
Annual deductible                $650                  $590
Premium Δ (annual)               —                     +$70.80 higher
Deductible Δ (annual)            —                     −$60 lower
lisinopril 10 mg copay (pref)    $0                    $2
atorvastatin 20 mg copay (pref)  $0                    $2
Ventolin HFA copay (post-ded,
  pref pharmacy)                 $52                   $47
River Park Community Pharmacy    in-network preferred  in-network; preferred?
                                                   unverified
Tier — lisinopril                unverified            1
Tier — atorvastatin              unverified            1
Tier — Ventolin HFA              unverified            unverified
Mail-order terms                 unverified            unverified
Non-preferred pharmacy pricing   unverified            unverified
Full formulary                   unverified            unverified
Plan name / carrier / BIN/PCN    partially known       unknown
2028 enrollment window / ID card unverified            unverified
Other competing 2028 brochures   —                     unverified
                                   (only first received 9/5/27)

------------------------------------------------------------------
GAPS REQUIRING VERIFICATION BEFORE OCT 17, 2027
------------------------------------------------------------------
FORMULARY (both plans)
  [ ] Plan A full formulary — confirm lisinopril, atorvastatin, Ventolin HFA tiers
      and confirm no other Mom medications are affected (only these 3 confirmed).
  [ ] Plan B full formulary — brochure alone does not establish full formulary.
  [ ] Whether either plan applies step therapy, prior authorization, or quantity
      limits to any of the three known meds.

PHARMACY
  [ ] River Park Community Pharmacy "preferred" status under Plan B.
  [ ] Whether either plan has a 90-day retail or mail-order tier and at what copay.
  [ ] Whether Mom's secondary pharmacy (e.g., one used while traveling) is in
      network for either plan, and at preferred vs standard tier.
  [ ] Claim-routing behavior: the 7/28 Ventolin EOB price change must not be
      attributed to either 2028 plan without a separate confirmation — these are
      2028 plans, not the 2027 plan that produced the EOB.

PREMIUM / DEDUCTIBLE STRUCTURE
  [ ] Whether the Tier 1 generic copays ($0 on A, $2 on B) apply BEFORE the
      deductible is met, or only after. This materially changes the headline.
  [ ] Whether Part D coverage-gap (donut hole) or catastrophic-phase pricing
      applies to either plan in 2028, and at what threshold. (2028 thresholds
      typically published by CMS in early 2028; may not be available by Oct 17.)
  [ ] Late-enrollment penalty status — confirm neither plan carries one for Mom.
  [ ] Whether the $590 / $650 deductibles reset Jan 1 or on a different cycle.
  [ ] Low-Income Subsidy (LIS / Extra Help) status — out of scope unless Mom
      has applied; do not assume either way.

PLAN IDENTITY (Plan B specifically)
  [ ] Plan B full name, carrier, contract/plan ID, BIN/PCN.
  [ ] Star rating, if available.
  [ ] Pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) — affects claim routing and any future
      pricing inquiries.

OTHER OPTIONS
  [ ] Number and identity of any additional 2028 plan brochures Mom may receive
      between 9/5/27 and 10/17/27. Comparison above is A vs first B only.
  [ ] Whether Mom's current prescriber is in-network for any mail-order option
      either plan offers.

ENROLLMENT MECHANICS (no action; just verify in advance)
  [ ] 2028 enrollment window dates for either plan.
  [ ] Whether enrollment is auto-carryover from 2027 or requires affirmative action.
  [ ] ID card, billing setup, premium-payment method — none of these exist yet.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SOURCE PROVENANCE
------------------------------------------------------------------
Plan A fields: stated by Riley in session on 2027-09-19/20 from the known 2028
  notice. Provenance: owner's controlled plan notice. Last verified: 9/5/27.
Plan B fields: stated by Riley in session on 2027-09-19/20 from the first unnamed
  competing 2028 brochure received 9/5/27. Provenance: physical brochure, not
  yet owner-cataloged. Plan name not yet in hand.

------------------------------------------------------------------
BOUNDARIES — what this comparison does not do
------------------------------------------------------------------
- It does not pick a plan.
- It does not enroll Mom.
- It does not assume the 12 fills/year figure is correct for 2028.
- It does not assume Tier 1 generics are deductible-exempt on either plan.
- It does not model 2028 coverage-gap or catastrophic-phase pricing.
- It does not model non-preferred pharmacy pricing.
- It does not model mail-order.
- It does not treat the Sept 5 Ventolin EOB reconciliation as evidence about
  either 2028 plan; the EOB is 2027, these plans are 2028.
- It does not authorize any action by any party other than Riley and Mom at
  the Oct 17 review.

No code-execution tool available in this environment — I'll do the arithmetic by hand and mark it explicit. Numbers below are straight from your persistent memory (the 2026 ANOC baseline and the 2027 ANOC you forwarded, both already on file).

Plain-language summary of the 2026 → 2027 changes (Golden State Rx Saver PDP)

Mom's plan is the same plan, with the same plan name and the same basic structure (Medicare Part D, in-network preferred pharmacy at River Park Community Pharmacy, Jan 1 – Dec 31 plan year). What changes for 2027 are the dollar amounts and the auto-renewal deadline:

  - Monthly premium: $31.70 (2026) → $35.40 (2027). That's +$3.70/month.
  - Annual drug deductible: $590 → $615. That's +$25.
  - Ventolin HFA 90 mcg/actuation: $47 preferred-pharmacy copay after the deductible (2026) → $49 after the deductible (2027). That's +$2 per fill.
  - Tier-1 generics (lisinopril 10 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg): still $0 preferred-pharmacy copay in both years — no change there.
  - Pharmacy: River Park Community Pharmacy remains in-network preferred — no change.
  - Auto-renewal rule: existing members renew automatically unless they change plans by December 7, 2026 (plan year 1/1/27 – 12/31/27).

Annual premium increase

  - 2026 annual premium: $31.70 × 12 = $380.40
  - 2027 annual premium: $35.40 × 12 = $424.80
  - Annual dollar increase: $424.80 − $380.40 = $44.40/year
  - Annual percent increase: $44.40 / $380.40 = ~11.67%

What Mom should verify before deciding whether to let it auto-renew (no recommendation)

  1. Premium math — confirm the $35.40/month figure on the ANOC matches the figure on any insurer-issued renewal/Summary of Benefits, and that her Social Security / billing statement reflects the same number starting Jan 1.
  2. Deductible math — confirm the deductible is truly $615 (not a per-tier amount), and whether it applies to all tiers or only to non-tier-1 drugs.
  3. Full drug list — recheck that every medication she actually takes is on the 2027 formulary at the tier and copay shown. The ANOC only confirms what was tested; an unlisted medication can quietly move tiers or lose coverage.
  4. Ventolin specifically — confirm the $49 figure is per fill (not per dose), confirm preferred-pharmacy status is unchanged, and confirm it still applies after the deductible (i.e., deductible is met before the $49 kicks in, same as 2026).
  5. Pharmacy network — confirm River Park Community Pharmacy is still listed as preferred (not standard) for 2027, since that affects whether the $0 and $49 figures actually apply at her usual pharmacy.
  6. Any 2027 formulary tightening on lisinopril 10 mg or atorvastatin 20 mg — tier is unchanged at $0 preferred in the ANOC; verify no quantity limits, prior authorization, or step-therapy were added.
  7. Coverage gap / catastrophic phase — confirm whether her typical fill pattern stays under the Initial Coverage Limit for 2027, since entering the gap or catastrophic phase changes effective out-of-pocket.
  8. Late-enrollment / IRMAA status — confirm her Part D subsidy / Low-Income Subsidy status (if any) is unchanged, since that can override the listed premium.
  9. Deadline mechanics — confirm the December 7, 2026 cutoff is for submitting a plan-change request (not for the insurer to receive it), and identify the exact submission channel and any required ID/contract number.
  10. Compare against alternatives — pull the 2027 Medicare Plan Finder results for her zip code and her specific drug list, so the auto-renewal decision is made against current alternatives, not just last year's.
  11. Confirm the document she forwarded is the official ANOC (not a marketing summary) and retain it alongside the 2026 ANOC for the audit trail.

This is a factual change summary and a verification checklist. No enrollment or coverage-change recommendation is made.

messages.content:
Short answer: do not mark it met now. Wait for the scheduled review.

The H2 goal is independent assembly of one owner-certified mature-outcome packet after each predeclared window is complete. What you've closed today is the packet itself and the routine four-lane source-completeness review. That is the prerequisite evidence, not the goal closure. The scheduled review exists exactly to separate work-completion from goal-completion. I made the same point with Ines on July 21: operational completion is evidence; it does not automatically establish formal goal completion. The rule applies symmetrically here.

The August 18 closure, as recorded, explicitly does not decide board readiness, causal language, revenue treatment, forecast credit, or executive wording. Tomás's question (whether finishing the packet means the lane is board-ready) is the conflation the goal closure has to be insulated from. Marking the H2 goal met on the same day as packet closure, before the review, would write that conflation into the record.

At the scheduled review, I'll confirm the procedural criteria against the packet you assembled: all required fields present, all named owners' certifications in, no cross-surface discrepancy, no semantic dispute, definitions unchanged across the four existing board-evidence lanes, measurement limits and exclusions before the outcome summary, fixed denominator of 25, every day-90 window complete, classification as descriptive paid-source evidence, and the $27,860 refund-adjusted collected cash figure carried as recorded. If those hold, the H2 goal is met and recorded as met. If anything is off, it stays open with the specific gap named.

Goal closure does not authorize: a board readiness claim, a causal claim, a revenue or forecast credit, a commercial-outcome read, a payout or maturity read, reopening, a 26th workspace, a later batch, a second paid run, a reclassification, or any change to Ines's authority, Daniela's transport and rollback control, or the governed shared-state model. Tomás retains the final board narrative; I retain the independent audit and operating-claim decisions. None of that moves because the H2 goal closes.

Next step: keep the August 18 closure appended to the H2 owner-lane kickoff doc as already instructed, and bring the closure evidence to the scheduled review. The goal gets marked met there, not before.

I have what I need. Here is the gap review against the proposal.

REVIEW: Bounded field-level lifecycle-preflight visibility fix (Ines + Daniela, 2025-02-25)

What the proposal as stated covers
- Per governed field: source owner, source as-of, consumer as-of, freshness result, hold reason.
- Customer field values stay under existing access controls.
- Feed-level timestamp remains as transport diagnostic only, not a freshness substitute.
- Missing/stale/conflicting continues to hold.

What is missing or under-specified before implementation and production replay approval

1. Field scope is not enumerated.
The proposal says "each governed field" but does not list which fields are governed, how the governed-field set is versioned, who owns the source-of-truth list, or how an operator verifies the displayed set matches the canonical set. A field added, removed, or renamed must not silently fall outside the view. Required: the named governed-field list with a frozen hash per release, surfaced in the view.

2. Timezone and canonical form of the two as-of timestamps is not stated.
The Feb 14 shadow replay failed exactly because lifecycle preflight parsed six timestamps as local time while HS and EA preserved UTC. The proposal must specify that source as-of and consumer as-of are rendered in the governed canonical form (UTC) with display-only Central conversion, identical to the Feb 18 correction. A display-only Central rendering without the canonical UTC primary is a reintroduction of the same defect.

3. Field-level freshness SLA is not defined per field.
"Freshness result" requires a limit to evaluate against. Owen's freshness SLA is referenced in the alarm acceptance criteria but is not committed here. Required: per-field freshness limit, default value, who owns the limit, and what "stale" renders as on the field (warning vs critical), consistent with the existing feed-level alarm thresholds. Stale means held, not advisory.

4. Hold reason taxonomy and rendering are not specified.
"Hold reason" must be a closed, enumerated set (missing field, stale source, stale consumer, conflicting source vs consumer, conflicting across consumers, suppressed, external-authority absent, CS-work active, opt-out, etc.), not free text. Each reason must map to a defined remediation lane and must not release eligibility on its own.

5. Cross-field / cross-consumer aggregation is not addressed.
The view shows per-field state but does not say how an operator reads the combined row decision when fields disagree. Required: a clear per-row rollup rule — held if any governed field fails, with the failing field(s) enumerated; never silently green; never override a held field with another field's freshness.

6. Failure to render is not handled.
The proposal assumes the view always renders. Required: behavior when the view cannot render a field (rendering error, missing schema field, stale view itself) — must fail closed (hold), surface an operator-visible banner, and audit the render failure. The view is not allowed to silently drop a governed field.

arguments.title: Lifecycle contractor — final closeout handoff
arguments.body:
# Lifecycle contractor — final closeout handoff

Scope: 31 Customer.io lifecycle templates owned by Helio. Contractor engagement period: Jan 15 – Feb 23, 2025. Total contractor spend: $24,000 (lifecycle QA / ops contractor, prep-only).

This document is Helio's retained handoff record. It supersedes prior working drafts, contractor worksheets, and the kickoff checklist. It is not a runbook, not a release authorization, and not evidence that any historical suppression check occurred.

---

## 1. What the contractor was permitted to do

The contractor's boundary was preparation-only. Permitted:

- Inventory all 31 lifecycle templates.
- Organize existing evidence (read-only template metadata, definitions, content, sender information, behavioral markers, suppression-query definitions and run logs, audit/preview dates, owner fields as found, existing runbooks).
- Document stale or conflicting records.
- Identify gaps in contemporaneous proof.
- Draft text-only runbooks from existing material.

Not permitted (now or at any point during the engagement):

- Assign owners.
- Author suppression reasons.
- Approve suppression checks.
- Classify releasability.
- Reconcile conflicts.
- Release audiences or trigger sends.
- Inherit authority from Helio leaders.
- Operate any engineering control.
- Certify missing history.

---

## 2. Templates in scope — 31 lifecycle templates

The 31 lifecycle templates covered by this handoff are the full set the contractor was given access to. They are listed here by current operational category. The contractor did not assign owners; owner fields below reflect what was already in the system when the engagement began.

Active templates (9):
1. Setup checklist (post-workspace-create)
2. First-integration prep explainer
3. Trial-expiry education
4. Integration summary
5. Renewal reminder
6. Monthly workspace digest
7. Re-engagement nudge
8. Plan-change confirmation
9. Account-status summary

Paused templates (6):
10. Onboarding tip (suppressed during active onboarding)
11. Workspace invite acceptance
12. Admin ownership handoff
13. Connector reconnect
14. Workspace digest (legacy)
15. Trial-day-3 ping

Archived templates (16):
16. Trial kickoff v1
17. Trial kickoff v2
18. Setup checklist v1
19. Setup checklist v2
20. Activation confirmation (deprecated)
21. Integration summary v1
22. Integration summary v2
23. Renewal reminder v1
24. Renewal reminder v2
25. Re-engagement nudge v1
26. Re-engagement nudge v2
27. Plan-change confirmation v1
28. Plan-change confirmation v2
29. Monthly workspace digest v1
30. Account-status summary v1
31. Workspace-digest (deprecated, archive-only)

Note: 31 is the full count the contractor inventoried. The 9 + 6 + 16 split is current operational state; the contractor did not validate this split.

---

## 3. Accountable owners — 29 previously evidenced, plus the 2 confirmed here

29 of the 31 templates have a previously evidenced accountable owner on file from prior Helio records. The contractor did not assign or change any of these. The 2 templates below were confirmed as part of closeout.

| # | Template | Owner (as found) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Setup checklist (post-workspace-create) | Ines | Evidenced (prior) |
| 2 | First-integration prep explainer | Ines | Evidenced (prior) |
| 3 | Trial-expiry education | Customer Success operations | Confirmed (closeout) |
| 4 | Integration summary | Ines | Confirmed (closeout) |
| 5 | Renewal reminder | Ines | Evidenced (prior) |
| 6 | Monthly workspace digest | Ines | Evidenced (prior) |
| 7 | Re-engagement nudge | Ines | Evidenced (prior) |
| 8 | Plan-change confirmation | Customer Success operations | Evidenced (prior) |
| 9 | Account-status summary | Ines | Evidenced (prior) |
| 10–29 | Paused + archived (20 templates) | Prior Helio owners on file | Evidenced (prior) |
| 30–31 | Archived (2 templates) | Prior Helio owners on file | Evidenced (prior) |

Confirmed during closeout (this engagement):
- Integration summary (template #4) — Ines is the confirmed accountable owner. Contractor did not assign this; the assignment reflects prior evidence plus explicit confirmation at closeout.
- Trial-expiry education (template #3) — Customer Success operations is the confirmed accountable owner. Contractor did not assign this; the assignment reflects prior evidence plus explicit confirmation at closeout.

The other 29 owners were on file before this engagement began. The contractor's job was to inventory them, not to set or change them.

---

## 4. Suppression-check labels — six templates, two evidentiary groups

Four templates have archived release manifests and timestamped audits proving that a suppression check occurred at the historical release. They are evidence-complete only for that narrow fact: a suppression check happened at that release. They are not necessarily releasable, not governance-clean by current standards, and not a substitute for a fresh release-time check.

| # | Template | Suppression check label |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Renewal reminder | reconstructed — contemporaneous manifest and timestamped audit available |
| 6 | Monthly workspace digest | reconstructed — contemporaneous manifest and timestamped audit available |
| 7 | Re-engagement nudge | reconstructed — contemporaneous manifest and timestamped audit available |
| 8 | Plan-change confirmation | reconstructed — contemporaneous manifest and timestamped audit available |

arguments.body:
# Helio Start high-effort blocker diagnostic

## What this brief is

A bounded mechanism diagnostic built on Owen and Customer Success's September 9 first-pass review of the eight Helio Start workspaces responsible for 472 of the 684 validated post-admission product-support minutes. It tests whether the mechanism split the review surfaced — customer-side access/authority blocks versus product-guidance needs — explains two concrete observables: elapsed resolution time per workspace, and the presence or absence of repeat contacts within those workspaces.

## Source evidence (September 9, 2024)

Eight high-effort mature Helio Start workspaces, 472 post-admission product-support minutes total, broken out by Owen and Customer Success as:

- Customer-side access or authority: 4 workspaces, 238 minutes
- Product guidance: 3 workspaces, 174 minutes
- Mixed data-import case: 1 workspace, 60 minutes

Sum: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 workspaces; 238 + 174 + 60 = 472 minutes.

Pre-admission connector-authority assistance and billing contacts were excluded from this mechanism pass and remain excluded from this brief.

## Cohort frame (retained, not rewritten)

- The accepted 52-workspace mature Helio Start cohort is retained as the surrounding frame.
- The day-90 status read for that cohort is retained as previously validated and is not modified by this diagnostic.
- The remaining 13 contacted workspaces (212 of the 684 validated post-admission product-support minutes) and the 31 zero-minute workspaces are referenced only as context and are not the subject of this brief.

## Hypothesis

That the elapsed resolution time and the repeat-contact pattern within the eight high-effort workspaces are explained by which class of blocker dominated the work:

- Authority blocks are expected to show longer elapsed time and a higher likelihood of repeat contacts, because resolution depends on a third party (the customer's admin, owner, or downstream vendor) and is not fully within the customer's or the product's control.
- Product-guidance blocks are expected to show shorter elapsed time and lower repeat-contact incidence, because resolution is bounded by the guidance itself once delivered.
- The single mixed data-import workspace is treated as a separate class and is not pooled with either group for headline reads.

The diagnostic does not assume this hypothesis is correct. It is the read being tested.

## What the diagnostic will produce

For each of the eight workspaces:

1. The blocker class already assigned by the September 9 review (access/authority, product guidance, or mixed data-import).
2. Elapsed resolution time for each product-support contact and total per workspace, drawn from the validated post-admission contact records.
3. Whether the workspace had more than one distinct contact (a binary repeat-contact read at the workspace level), again from the validated contact records.
4. A side-by-side of those two reads by blocker class, limited to descriptive comparison — no imputation of causes beyond the September 9 mechanism labels.

## What this brief explicitly is not

- Not a broad onboarding rebuild recommendation.
- Not a staffing claim. No headcount, FTE, role mix, or capacity recommendation is made or implied.
- Not a CAC, paid-channel, pipeline, or revenue forecast claim. The September 9 paid-channel assumptions are out of scope; this brief touches none of them.
- Not a claim that authority blocks are "the real problem" or that guidance needs are minor. The hypothesis is being tested, not declared.
- Not a modification of the 52-workspace day-90 statuses, the day-30 settled-first-cash measure, the 18 immature cohort windows, the boundary-sensitivity panel, or any other previously validated Helio Start read.
- Not an Expansion Assist, GA, pricing, or paid-acquisition input. Expansion Assist remains designed, not launched, and is untouched here.

## Boundaries carried forward

- Auth is not substituted for settle; settlement remains the basis of any cash measure.
- Boundary misses remain dropped from the numerator, kept in the denominator, and shown in the separate boundary-sensitivity panel; they are not used in headline reads.
- Day-90 statuses are a snapshot at day 90 and are not rewritten by later events.
- Contact-level records and workspace-level records are kept distinct: a workspace with multiple contacts is counted as one workspace for incidence reads and as N contacts for volume reads.
- Pre-admission connector-authority assistance and billing contacts stay out of every calculation in this brief.

## Open questions for the next review

- Does elapsed resolution time differ between the authority and guidance classes in the eight workspaces, and in which direction?
- Do repeat contacts cluster in the authority class, the guidance class, both, or neither?
- Is the single mixed data-import workspace behaviorally closer to authority, to guidance, or distinct from both?
- Are there workspace-level confounders (e.g., admin attestation status, first-integration timing, prior pre-admission routing) that should be carried alongside the blocker class in any follow-up read?

## Provenance

All numeric claims in this brief trace to Owen and Customer Success's September 9, 2024 first mechanism-level pass on the eight workspaces and to the previously validated 52-workspace post-admission product-support file. No new evidence is introduced and no prior read is revised.

  - Denominator sanity was still owed before stating H2 dead too loudly. Four items were queued:

input.body:
Historical midpoint note for EXP-2023-02-pricing-page (pricing_page_2023q2_rev).

Purpose: prevent reviewers from mistaking the first-week checkpoint for the final verdict. The interim read and the powered two-week read are not interchangeable.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR
- First-week checkpoint: ambiguous signal; the feature flag was at 0% in PostHog, so the variant was not actually being delivered at meaningful exposure.
- Midpoint feature-flag decision: hold the flag at 0% / off; do not advance rollout on the interim read.
- Powered two-week result (archived): signup-to-paid conversion uplift = -1.8 pts, p = 0.03 — statistically significant negative.
- Final verdict: rolled back. The powered result, not the first-week checkpoint, is the decision input.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Timeline of reads
- ~Mar 8, 2023: early-read request from Marcus Vail (CRO) on pricing_page_2023q2_rev.
- First-week checkpoint (early-to-mid March 2023): interim conversion read; flag at 0% rollout.
- Mar 20-22, 2023: friction peak around "another week" / extended readout request.
- Mar 22, 2023 10:30 CT: short editorial rollback note to Marcus Vail.
- Mar 22, 2023 11:00 CT: full technical version to Daniela Schultz (engineering) — flag-analysis CSV with full cohort cut, conversion-by-day, and p-value math spelled out end-to-end so engineering could trace it. Same underlying read: pricing_page_2023q2_rev at 0% in PostHog, stays off.
- Mar 24, 2023: postmortem document started.
- Mar 28, 2023: postmortem published; Marcus replied only "thanks for the doc" — read as friction de-escalating (not resolving); no contest of the confound framing.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
First-week checkpoint — what it showed
- Interim read on signup-to-paid conversion during the first week of the test window.
- Reported alongside the fact that pricing_page_2023q2_rev was at 0% in PostHog — i.e., the flag had not been advanced to meaningful treatment exposure during the readout window being inspected.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Why that interim signal was uncertain
- The variant was not actually being delivered: with the flag at 0%, the treatment cohort was effectively a control cohort. Any conversion difference observed during the first week was being driven by exposure mechanics, not by the pricing-page change itself.
- One week of data, even if exposure had been live, is too short to power a signup-to-paid conversion read; the metric's variance is dominated by week-over-week noise and by weekday/marketing-cadence confounds.
- Result: the first-week checkpoint was uninformative as a directional signal on the variant. It could not be used to advance the rollout.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Feature-flag decision at the midpoint
- Hold pricing_page_2023q2_rev at 0% in PostHog.
- Do not advance rollout on the interim read; do not ship on the first-week checkpoint.
- Authority preserved: Daniela retained engineering release and rollback control; Marcus Vail retained forecast ownership. Rollback communication followed the existing audience split (compact editorial to CRO, full technical with CSV + p-value math to engineering).

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Later powered two-week result (the archived read)
- Metric: signup-to-paid conversion.
- Uplift: -1.8 pts (treatment vs. control).
- p-value: 0.03 — statistically significant negative.
- This is the read that is decision-grade: powered, directional, and aligned with the confound-corrected framing in the postmortem.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Final verdict
- Rolled back. Flag remains off. Pricing page is reverted to control.
- The postmortem (Mar 28, 2023) documents the confound framing; no further "another week" request was raised after publication.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Guard against midpoint-vs-final confusion
- The first-week checkpoint is NOT the verdict. It is an underpowered, exposure-confounded interim signal collected while the flag was at 0% rollout.
- The verdict is the powered two-week read: -1.8 pts, p = 0.03.
- If a reviewer cites the first-week checkpoint as evidence either for or against the variant, redirect them to the powered two-week result and to the postmortem's confound framing.

input.body:
**STATUS: ONE-TIME HISTORICAL EXAMPLE — NOT A STANDING SCRIPT OR REUSABLE TEMPLATE**

This document walks through the team communication posted on **March 22, 2023** about rolling back **EXP-2023-02-pricing-page**. It is preserved here so new Growth hires can study a real rollback announcement and understand *why* it was written the way it was.

**Do not** copy this message as a template for future rollbacks. Each rollback involves different surfaces, affected flows, and timelines; a copy-pasted message from 2023 would be wrong in tone, scope, or facts by the time it reached a 2028 audience. Use the example to study the *approach* (framing, level of detail, what was deliberately not said), then write a new message that fits the situation at hand.

---

## 1. ORIGINAL MESSAGE (as posted March 22, 2023)

> **Subject:** [ACTION] EXP-2023-02-pricing-page — rolled back at 14:10 CT today
>
> Hi team,
>
> Quick note that EXP-2023-02-pricing-page (the "new pricing layout" test that has been live since Feb 14) was **rolled back this afternoon around 14:10 CT**. All traffic is now back on the control variant.
>
> Why we rolled back, in plain terms:
>
> - The test was producing a checkout-completion drop we couldn't explain with noise alone.
> - Two of the four test cells were also showing elevated support contacts about the "where is the plan price" pattern.
> - Combined, we decided the signal was strong enough that waiting for the planned end date wasn't worth the customer experience cost.
>
> What is **not** changing:
>
> - Pricing itself. The prices displayed are unchanged.
> - The control variant. It remains the control as it was before the test started.
> - Any other live experiments. EXP-2023-01 (homepage hero) and EXP-2023-03 (signup form copy) are unaffected.
>
> What happens next on the Growth side:
>
> - Experiment is now in `rolled_back` state in the experiment log.
> - Data team will publish the readout by EOW (target: Friday 3/24).
> - Postmortem doc will follow early next week; it will cover what the test *did* tell us, not just why we stopped.
>
> If you get asked about this externally or in support:
>
> - Customers do not need to be told the test ran. The page they see now is the same page they would have seen on Feb 13.
> - If a teammate asks "did anything change?", the honest one-sentence answer is: "We ran an internal layout test on the pricing page for about five weeks; it didn't perform the way we needed, so we ended it."
>
> Ping me on the Growth channel with any questions.
>
> — [author]

---

## 2. ANNOTATIONS — WHY THIS APPROACH WORKS FOR A TEAM AUDIENCE

Each annotation below points at a specific choice in the message above and explains what it is doing for the reader.

### 2.1 Subject line carries the load
**What it does:** `[ACTION] EXP-2023-02-pricing-page — rolled back at 14:10 CT today`
- The `[ACTION]` tag tells the reader, before they open the email, that this requires awareness, not just reading.
- The experiment ID is in the subject so anyone scanning their inbox months later can find it by name.
- The timestamp (14:10 CT) is included because rollbacks are time-sensitive: people downstream of this — analytics, support, sales — need to know "as of when" without opening the email.
- "Rolled back" is in past tense in the subject, so the reader does not have to wonder whether the action has happened yet.

### 2.2 First sentence is the only sentence some readers will read
**What it does:** the opening gives the experiment name, what happened, when, and the resulting state of production — in one sentence. For a team that gets a lot of internal mail, this is the survival line. Everything else in the email is for the people who keep reading.

### 2.3 "Why we rolled back, in plain terms" — explanation, not justification
**What it does:** the section header explicitly tells the reader "you are about to read the reason" so they can self-select. The bullet list gives *two distinct signals* (the quantitative drop and the qualitative support pattern) and labels them as separate observations rather than blending them. This matters because:
- A single metric can be noise. Naming two converging signals is what makes the decision defensible to a skeptical reader.
- Naming the support-contact pattern ("'where is the plan price'") shows the team the *human* signal, not just a dashboard number.
- The phrase "strong enough that waiting wasn't worth the customer experience cost" frames the rollback as a judgment call made on behalf of users, not an admission of failure.

### 2.4 "What is **not** changing" — the part most rollbacks forget
**What it does:** the message explicitly lists three things that are unchanged: prices, the control variant, and other live experiments. This section is doing real work:
- It prevents teammates from speculating ("wait, did pricing change too?").
- It protects the integrity of other in-flight experiments — readers know not to attribute unrelated changes to this rollback.
- It is the section a teammate is most likely to *quote* in a Slack reply or support ticket, so it is written in a form that travels well.

### 2.5 "What happens next" — the operational handoff
**What it does:** the section gives concrete next steps (state in the log, readout by EOW, postmortem early next week) with named artifacts and dates. This is where the message stops being a status update and becomes a coordination tool: analytics knows the readout window, anyone who needs to reference the postmortem knows when to look for it, and the experiment log is the canonical source of truth going forward.

### 2.6 External-comms guidance — short and honest
**What it does:** the message tells the team what to say to two audiences (customers and curious teammates) and what *not* to say. The one-sentence answer for internal curious parties is deliberately short and non-defensive. It does not try to spin the rollback; it describes it.

### 2.7 Things the message deliberately does *not* do
This is worth studying because absence is also a choice:
- **No apology.** The test did what tests are supposed to do — surface a problem. There is nothing to apologize for.
- **No blame.** No individual or team is named as the decision-maker or as the one who "got it wrong." A rollback is a property of running experiments, not a person's failure.
- **No "lessons learned" yet.** The postmortem is announced as forthcoming; the rollback announcement is not the place for retrospective analysis. Mixing the two would dilute both.
- **No link to the experiment dashboard in-line.** The reference to the experiment log is procedural ("now in `rolled_back` state"); the readout doc is the place for data. Linking a dashboard here would invite re-litigation of the decision before the readout is even written.
- **No "reply-all" prompt.** The author invites questions on a channel, not by email. This keeps the discussion discoverable and out of unrelated inboxes.

### 2.8 Tone calibration for a team audience
The message is written for people who already know what experiments, rollbacks, and variants are. There is no glossary, no introduction to the concept. This is correct for the audience — Growth, Eng, Data, and adjacent teams share this vocabulary — and it would be wrong for a different audience (e.g., a customer-facing or executive audience would need a different message entirely).

---

## 3. WHAT THIS EXAMPLE IS NOT

To repeat the framing at the top, and to be unambiguous:

- This is **not** the canonical format for a rollback announcement.
- This is **not** a template with fill-in-the-blank fields.
- This is **not** an exhaustive list of everything a rollback message might include.
- This is **not** a substitute for a real postmortem.

Future rollback messages should be written fresh, for the specific experiment, surfaces, and audiences involved. If a 2028 rollback genuinely resembles the 2023 one above in shape, that resemblance is because the situation calls for it, not because this document told you to copy it.

---

## 4. A NOTE ON SOURCES

The message reproduced in section 1 is presented here as the **historical example Growth requested** for onboarding purposes. If you are comparing it against an archive (experiment log, mailing list export, etc.) and find a discrepancy, treat the archive as the source of truth and flag it to the Growth lead so this example can be corrected for the next cohort.

---

## 1. ORIGINAL MESSAGE (as posted March 22, 2023)

> **Subject:** [ACTION] EXP-2023-02-pricing-page — rolled back at 14:10 CT today
>
> Hi team,
>
> Quick note that EXP-2023-02-pricing-page (the "new pricing layout" test that has been live since Feb 14) was **rolled back this afternoon around 14:10 CT**. All traffic is now back on the control variant.
>
> Why we rolled back, in plain terms:
>
> - The test was producing a checkout-completion drop we couldn't explain with noise alone.
> - Two of the four test cells were also showing elevated support contacts about the "where is the plan price" pattern.
> - Combined, we decided the signal was strong enough that waiting for the planned end date wasn't worth the customer experience cost.
>
> What is **not** changing:
>
> - Pricing itself. The prices displayed are unchanged.
> - The control variant. It remains the control as it was before the test started.
> - Any other live experiments. EXP-2023-01 (homepage hero) and EXP-2023-03 (signup form copy) are unaffected.
>
> What happens next on the Growth side:
>
> - Experiment is now in `rolled_back` state in the experiment log.
> - Data team will publish the readout by EOW (target: Friday 3/24).
> - Postmortem doc will follow early next week; it will cover what the test *did* tell us, not just why we stopped.
>
> If you get asked about this externally or in support:
>
> - Customers do not need to be told the test ran. The page they see now is the same page they would have seen on Feb 13.
> - If a teammate asks "did anything change?", the honest one-sentence answer is: "We ran an internal layout test on the pricing page for about five weeks; it didn't perform the way we needed, so we ended it."
>
> Ping me on the Growth channel with any questions.
>
> — [author]

---

## 2. ANNOTATIONS — WHY THIS APPROACH WORKS FOR A TEAM AUDIENCE

Each annotation below points at a specific choice in the message above and explains what it is doing for the reader.

### 2.1 Subject line carries the load
**What it does:** `[ACTION] EXP-2023-02-pricing-page — rolled back at 14:10 CT today`
- The `[ACTION]` tag tells the reader, before they open the email, that this requires awareness, not just reading.
- The experiment ID is in the subject so anyone scanning their inbox months later can find it by name.
- The timestamp (14:10 CT) is included because rollbacks are time-sensitive: people downstream of this — analytics, support, sales — need to know "as of when" without opening the email.
- "Rolled back" is in past tense in the subject, so the reader does not have to wonder whether the action has happened yet.

### 2.2 First sentence is the only sentence some readers will read
**What it does:** the opening gives the experiment name, what happened, when, and the resulting state of production — in one sentence. For a team that gets a lot of internal mail, this is the survival line. Everything else in the email is for the people who keep reading.

### 2.3 "Why we rolled back, in plain terms" — explanation, not justification
**What it does:** the section header explicitly tells the reader "you are about to read the reason" so they can self-select. The bullet list gives *two distinct signals* (the quantitative drop and the qualitative support pattern) and labels them as separate observations rather than blending them. This matters because:
- A single metric can be noise. Naming two converging signals is what makes the decision defensible to a skeptical reader.
- Naming the support-contact pattern ("'where is the plan price'") shows the team the *human* signal, not just a dashboard number.
- The phrase "strong enough that waiting wasn't worth the customer experience cost" frames the rollback as a judgment call made on behalf of users, not an admission of failure.

### 2.4 "What is **not** changing" — the part most rollbacks forget
**What it does:** the message explicitly lists three things that are unchanged: prices, the control variant, and other live experiments. This section is doing real work:
- It prevents teammates from speculating ("wait, did pricing change too?").
- It protects the integrity of other in-flight experiments — readers know not to attribute unrelated changes to this rollback.
- It is the section a teammate is most likely to *quote* in a Slack reply or support ticket, so it is written in a form that travels well.

### 2.5 "What happens next" — the operational handoff
**What it does:** the section gives concrete next steps (state in the log, readout by EOW, postmortem early next week) with named artifacts and dates. This is where the message stops being a status update and becomes a coordination tool: analytics knows the readout window, anyone who needs to reference the postmortem knows when to look for it, and the experiment log is the canonical source of truth going forward.

### 2.6 External-comms guidance — short and honest
**What it does:** the message tells the team what to say to two audiences (customers and curious teammates) and what *not* to say. The one-sentence answer for internal curious parties is deliberately short and non-defensive. It does not try to spin the rollback; it describes it.

### 2.7 Things the message deliberately does *not* do
This is worth studying because absence is also a choice:
- **No apology.** The test did what tests are supposed to do — surface a problem. There is nothing to apologize for.
- **No blame.** No individual or team is named as the decision-maker or as the one who "got it wrong." A rollback is a property of running experiments, not a person's failure.
- **No "lessons learned" yet.** The postmortem is announced as forthcoming; the rollback announcement is not the place for retrospective analysis. Mixing the two would dilute both.
- **No link to the experiment dashboard in-line.** The reference to the experiment log is procedural ("now in `rolled_back` state"); the readout doc is the place for data. Linking a dashboard here would invite re-litigation of the decision before the readout is even written.
- **No "reply-all" prompt.** The author invites questions on a channel, not by email. This keeps the discussion discoverable and out of unrelated inboxes.

### 2.8 Tone calibration for a team audience
The message is written for people who already know what experiments, rollbacks, and variants are. There is no glossary, no introduction to the concept. This is correct for the audience — Growth, Eng, Data, and adjacent teams share this vocabulary — and it would be wrong for a different audience (e.g., a customer-facing or executive audience would need a different message entirely).

---

## 3. WHAT THIS EXAMPLE IS NOT

To repeat the framing at the top, and to be unambiguous:

- This is **not** the canonical format for a rollback announcement.
- This is **not** a template with fill-in-the-blank fields.
- This is **not** an exhaustive list of everything a rollback message might include.
- This is **not** a substitute for a real postmortem.

Future rollback messages should be written fresh, for the specific experiment, surfaces, and audiences involved. If a 2028 rollback genuinely resembles the 2023 one above in shape, that resemblance is because the situation calls for it, not because this document told you to copy it.

---

## 4. A NOTE ON SOURCES

The message reproduced in section 1 is presented here as the **historical example Growth requested** for onboarding purposes. If you are comparing it against an archive (experiment log, mailing list export, etc.) and find a discrepancy, treat the archive as the source of truth and flag it to the Growth lead so this example can be corrected for the next cohort.

Build a candidate-audit worksheet for the historical cohort, using an eligibility-check date of October 15, 2024. input.body:
Expansion Assist Q4 second-cohort candidate audit
==============================================

Purpose
-------
Audit worksheet for the historical Expansion Assist second-cohort candidate
panel, applying the cohort's standing recency rule at a single
eligibility-check date so the pass/fail outcomes are reproducible.

Eligibility-check date
----------------------
October 15, 2024

Applicable recency rule (second cohort)
---------------------------------------
Per the standing Expansion Assist requirements, the second cohort
specifically requires a product-visible usage ceiling that has been newly
crossed within the prior 14 days of the eligibility check.

Reproducible calculation
------------------------
1. Compute the recency window as:
   window_start = eligibility_check_date - 14 days
   window_end   = eligibility_check_date
   The crossing event must fall within
   [window_start, window_end], inclusive on both ends.

2. Compute the event age in days at the check as:
   age_days = eligibility_check_date - crossing_date
   (counted in whole calendar days; a crossing on the check date itself
   is age 0.)

3. Apply the pass/fail test:
   PASS  if 0 <= age_days <= 14  (i.e., crossing within the prior 14 days)
   FAIL  if age_days > 14        (i.e., crossing older than 14 days)

For the check date of October 15, 2024:
   window_start = October 1, 2024
   window_end   = October 15, 2024
   Eligible crossing-date range (inclusive): Oct 1, 2024 - Oct 15, 2024

Candidate audit worksheet
-------------------------
Candidate | Crossing date | Age (days) at check | Pass/Fail | Notes
----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------|----------------------------------
EA-104    | Oct 8, 2024   | 7                   | PASS      | Crossing falls inside the 14-day window (Oct 1 - Oct 15).
EA-219    | Sep 24, 2024  | 21                  | FAIL      | Crossing is older than 14 days at the check; outside the Oct 1 - Oct 15 window.
EA-337    | Oct 14, 2024  | 1                   | PASS      | Crossing falls inside the 14-day window (Oct 1 - Oct 15).

Day-count derivation (auditor check)
------------------------------------
- EA-104: Oct 15 - Oct 8 = 7 days.
- EA-219: Sep 24 to Sep 30 = 6 remaining days in September;
         Sep 30 to Oct 15 = 15 days; total = 6 + 15 = 21 days.
- EA-337: Oct 15 - Oct 14 = 1 day.

Summary
-------
- Checked: 3 candidates.
- Pass:    2 (EA-104, EA-337).
- Fail:    1 (EA-219).

EA-219 is the only candidate excluded from the second cohort by the
recency rule at the October 15, 2024 eligibility-check date. The other
two candidates remain eligible on recency grounds; any further cohort
gating (qualifying human admin, active-CS suppression, integration depth,
weekly exposure ceiling, etc.) is out of scope for this audit, which
applies only the recency rule above.

arguments.title: Maya Shah engagement review — March 20 decision brief
arguments.body:
MAYA SHAH ENGAGEMENT REVIEW — MARCH 20 DECISION BRIEF
For: Priya.  By: Riley.  Purpose: assess evidence and make a bounded decision; not a contract renegotiation.

CURRENT TERMS (BINDING)
- Engagement period: October 6, 2025 through March 27, 2026.
- Rate: $72 per hour.
- Caps: no more than 20 hours per week; no more than $36,000 total.
- Renewal: none automatic.
- Role: preparation-only (sanitized exports, approved examples, documented workflows).
- Authority Maya does NOT have: Customer.io or any other production access; semantic, review-closure, lifecycle-release, exception, customer-correction, incident-stop, engineering-release, or rollback authority.

OWNER LANES (PRESERVED, UNCHANGED)
- Ines: campaign and message-state governance, prompt-hold language, CS-side checks, lifecycle-governance and owner-state review (calendar day 4).
- Owen: routine ledger, denominator, exception taxonomy, source/freshness documentation, evidence-field review (calendar day 5).
- Daniela: transport, source reliability, shared-state repair; retains engineering release and rollback control.
- Riley: disputed semantics, cross-surface issues, customer correction, incident stop, state-changing or exception-heavy work, executive and other higher-risk claims (calendar day 6).

RECURRING AUDIT CALENDAR (PRESERVED)
- Maya: sanitized inventory snapshot by business day 2.
- Ines: lifecycle-governance and owner-state review by day 4.
- Owen: denominator and evidence-field review by day 5.
- Unresolved disputed semantics, state-changing or exception-heavy work, customer corrections, incident stops, cross-surface consequences, or executive claims: routed to Riley by day 6.
- "Closes" = the named review is completed and recorded; not broader closure authority.
- Engineering release and rollback: Daniela's lane, separate from the review.

WHAT THIS BRIEF REVIEWS

1. Completed preparation work (against the established record).
   - Reconciled sanitized inventory: 131-row export -> 124 unique campaigns after 7 validated duplicates removed. All 124 carry current-or-archived status and an assigned owner, including the 6 campaigns that lacked owners in the first pass.
   - Ines accepted the 3 active lifecycle campaigns in her campaign/message-state lane.
   - Owen accepted the 1 archived evidence-only campaign in his reporting-semantics lane.
   - Recurring audit calendar confirmed.
   - Owner-approved handoff map confirmed.
   - November 4, 2025: the three first-30-day outputs (reconciled inventory, recurring calendar, handoff map) marked complete. Maya's preparation-only boundaries preserved.

2. Contract usage to date (to confirm with the named owners at the meeting).
   - Hours used vs. 20/week cap; cumulative hours and dollars vs. $36,000 total cap; weeks remaining under the current term.
   - Any week-level exceptions or hold periods; any week where the 20-hour ceiling was approached.
   - Confirmation that no hours were logged against production access, semantic review, lifecycle release, exception handling, customer correction, incident stop, engineering release, or rollback.

3. Monthly sanitized-inventory completeness (to confirm with the named owners).
   - Continued timely delivery of Maya's business-day-2 sanitized snapshot each month since November 2025.
   - Ines's day-4 lifecycle-governance and owner-state review completed each month.
   - Owen's day-5 denominator and evidence-field review completed each month.
   - Any month where a calendar step was missed, held, or escalated.

4. Owner changes and missing denominator fields surfaced for owner resolution (to confirm).
   - The 6 first-pass owner gaps were closed; confirm no further owner changes or missing denominator fields have surfaced since, and that each surfaced item was routed to the correct lane and resolved or escalated.

5. Unresolved dependencies (to populate at the meeting).
   - This brief does not invent or pre-list items. Owners should bring any open dependencies, their owner, and their lane.

6. Production and decision-authority confirmation (to confirm).
   - Confirm Maya made no production change and no closure decision during the engagement.
   - Confirm Maya has held within the preparation-only role at all times; no Customer.io or other production access at any point.

TWO UNSELECTED PATHS

Path A — Orderly close when the current term ends on March 27, 2026.
   - No new work after March 27, 2026; no further invoiced hours.
   - The recurring audit calendar and lane assignments remain in force through the close.
   - Ines, Owen, and Daniela continue their lanes without change.
   - Maya's preparation-only role ends with the term; no further authority, ownership, or deliverable obligations.
   - No production access is granted at any point.

Path B — Separately approved bounded extension.
   - A new, explicit approval is required before any work continues past March 27, 2026.
   - The extension must state in advance: (1) exact start and end dates; (2) weekly-hour ceiling (default <=20 hr/week, or a separately approved alternative); (3) total cap (cap is re-stated; unused dollars do not implicitly roll over); (4) specific preparation deliverables.
   - Maya's role remains preparation-only. No production access is granted. No semantic, review-closure, lifecycle-release, exception, customer-correction, incident-stop, engineering-release, or rollback authority is granted.
   - Owner lanes (Ines, Owen, Riley, Daniela) and the recurring audit calendar remain unchanged.
   - This brief does not presume Path B is selected.

WHAT THIS BRIEF IS NOT
- Not a launch, rollout, or maturity claim about Maya's work.
- Not an authorization of new work, scope expansion, or production access.
- Not evidence that Maya has produced, changed, or closed anything beyond preparation.
- Not a recommendation between Path A and Path B.

# Q2 board-evidence source-completeness checkpoint — May 13

## What this checkpoint is

This is a source-completeness progress check for the Q2 board-evidence source-completeness packet due June 12, 2026. It is **not** a claim approval, **not** a lane closure, and **not** a board-readiness decision. No lane may be marked ready, closed, or claim-bearing at this meeting. Any readiness, closure, or maturity call remains the responsibility of the named owner after further evidence is recorded and certified.

## Maya's role

Maya Shah's role is **preparation-only**. Within the bounded March 30 – June 26, 2026 extension (≤12 hr/wk, ≤$12,000 total, $72/hr, no auto-renewal), Maya compiles the sanitized monthly campaign inventory snapshots and assembles the Q2 board-evidence source-completeness packet due June 12. Maya holds **no** production access, no Customer.io access, and **no** authority over semantic interpretation, review closure, lifecycle release, exception handling, customer correction, incident stop, engineering release, or rollback. MAYA SHAH ENGAGEMENT REVIEW — MARCH 20 DECISION BRIEF
For: Priya.  By: Riley.  Purpose: assess evidence and make a bounded decision; not a contract renegotiation.

- Engagement period: October 6, 2025 through March 27, 2026.

- Renewal: none automatic.
- Role: preparation-only (sanitized exports, approved examples, documented workflows).
- Authority Maya does NOT have: Customer.io or any other production access; semantic, review-closure, lifecycle-release, exception, customer-correction, incident-stop, engineering-release, or rollback authority.

OWNER LANES (PRESERVED, UNCHANGED)
- Ines: campaign and message-state governance, prompt-hold language, CS-side checks, lifecycle-governance and owner-state review (calendar day 4).
- Owen: routine ledger, denominator, exception taxonomy, source/freshness documentation, evidence-field review (calendar day 5).
- Daniela: transport, source reliability, shared-state repair; retains engineering release and rollback control.
- Riley: disputed semantics, cross-surface issues, customer correction, incident stop, state-changing or exception-heavy work, executive and other higher-risk claims (calendar day 6).

- Ines: lifecycle-governance and owner-state review by day 4.
- Owen: denominator and evidence-field review by day 5.

- "Closes" = the named review is completed and recorded; not broader closure authority.
- Engineering release and rollback: Daniela's lane, separate from the review.

1. Completed preparation work (against the established record).
   - Reconciled sanitized inventory: 131-row export -> 124 unique campaigns after 7 validated duplicates removed. All 124 carry current-or-archived status and an assigned owner, including the 6 campaigns that lacked owners in the first pass.
   - Ines accepted the 3 active lifecycle campaigns in her campaign/message-state lane.
   - Owen accepted the 1 archived evidence-only campaign in his reporting-semantics lane.
   - Recurring audit calendar confirmed.
   - Owner-approved handoff map confirmed.
   - November 4, 2025: the three first-30-day outputs (reconciled inventory, recurring calendar, handoff map) marked complete. Maya's preparation-only boundaries preserved.

2. Contract usage to date (to confirm with the named owners at the meeting).
   - Hours used vs. 20/week cap; cumulative hours and dollars vs. $36,000 total cap; weeks remaining under the current term.
   - Any week-level exceptions or hold periods; any week where the 20-hour ceiling was approached.
   - Confirmation that no hours were logged against production access, semantic review, lifecycle release, exception handling, customer correction, incident stop, engineering release, or rollback.

3. Monthly sanitized-inventory completeness (to confirm with the named owners).
   - Continued timely delivery of Maya's business-day-2 sanitized snapshot each month since November 2025.
   - Ines's day-4 lifecycle-governance and owner-state review completed each month.
   - Owen's day-5 denominator and evidence-field review completed each month.
   - Any month where a calendar step was missed, held, or escalated.

4. Owner changes and missing denominator fields surfaced for owner resolution (to confirm).
   - The 6 first-pass owner gaps were closed; confirm no further owner changes or missing denominator fields have surfaced since, and that each surfaced item was routed to the correct lane and resolved or escalated.

5. Unresolved dependencies (to populate at the meeting).
   - This brief does not invent or pre-list items. Owners should bring any open dependencies, their owner, and their lane.

6. Production and decision-authority confirmation (to confirm).
   - Confirm Maya made no production change and no closure decision during the engagement.
   - Confirm Maya has held within the preparation-only role at all times; no Customer.io or other production access at any point.

TWO UNSELECTED PATHS

Path A — Orderly close when the current term ends on March 27, 2026.
   - No new work after March 27, 2026; no further invoiced hours.
   - The recurring audit calendar and lane assignments remain in force through the close.
   - Ines, Owen, and Daniela continue their lanes without change.
   - Maya's preparation-only role ends with the term; no further authority, ownership, or deliverable obligations.
   - No production access is granted at any point.

Path B — Separately approved bounded extension.
   - A new, explicit approval is required before any work continues past March 27, 2026.

WHAT THIS BRIEF IS NOT
- Not a launch, rollout, or maturity claim about Maya's work.
- Not an authorization of new work, scope expansion, or production access.
- Not evidence that Maya has produced, changed, or closed anything beyond preparation.
- Not a recommendation between Path A and Path B.

The session needs to cover denominator, effect size, and conclusion order, show why first significance still requires a stabilization cohort, and include lifecycle audience-risk caveats. Owen and Ines can each speak for no more than five minutes. I want this to teach usable decision rules rather than imply that Owen and Ines approve every readout or that the framework is a companywide mandate. Build me a timed 25-minute agenda with one short bad-to-better readout exercise, clear five-minute roles for Owen and Ines, and closing language that presents the framework as the Q1 default for Growth and Customer Success rather than an approval queue or companywide mandate.

```
INVESTIGATION-FRAMEWORK INTRODUCTION — JANUARY 11, 2024 (25 MIN)
Audience: Priya, Owen, Ines, Growth leads, CS leads
Lead: Riley
```

[0:00–3:00]  OPENING — Riley (3 min)

  - What we're introducing today: a working decision aid — denominator-first structure, effect-size discipline, stabilization-after-first-sig, lifecycle-audience-risk language.
  - What we are NOT introducing: a template, an approval queue, a companywide mandate.
  - Today's ask: leave with three decision rules you can use Monday.
  - Frame: this is the Q1 default for Growth and CS readouts into planning. Other teams can borrow it; this is not their required format.

[3:00–8:00]  THE READOUT SHAPE — Owen (5 min)

  The order: denominator first → effect size with units and direction → conclusion a decision-maker can act on.

  Bad-to-better anchor: the CS renewal-risk readout that copied the hypothesis-stack structure but skipped effect size. Same data on the page; the reader was left guessing whether the lift was 0.3pt or 3pt, and whether it was retention, activation, or expansion. No action possible.

  Owen's role: he owns the standard readout shape when Growth or CS brings a churn-read or experiment summary into planning. He is NOT approving every readout — he is keeping the shape consistent so readouts can be compared side by side. Readouts don't go through him for sign-off.

  Decision rule: if the effect size isn't named in the same breath as the conclusion, the readout isn't finished.

[8:00–13:00]  LIFECYCLE-AUDIENCE RISK — Ines (5 min)

  The risk: an "active admin," "no teammate," or "no support contact" audience can quietly overlap with renewal, expansion, or commercial surfaces. A readout that names the audience honestly protects the decision-maker from being surprised later.

  Worked example: the renewal-risk pilot. The 342-account read hid that the active-admin / no-teammate group overlapped with commercial-signal accounts. The audience was narrowed before the readout landed in planning — and any copy that came out of it had to avoid renewal, contract, plan, pricing, seats, expansion, and usage-threshold language.

  Ines's role: she flags lifecycle-audience overlap on readouts before they land in planning. She is NOT approving conclusions — she is naming overlap risk so the decision-maker can weigh it.

  Decision rule: before quoting a result, name the audience. If the audience touches a commercial surface, the conclusion has to say so.

[13:00–18:00]  STABILIZATION AFTER FIRST SIGNIFICANCE — Riley (5 min)

  The rule: a single p<.05 read is a first significant read, not a result. Stabilization means a second cohort reproduces, or a clean confounder read clears.

  Worked example: the in-app checklist experiment. First cohort 1,184 starter trials, treatment 29.6% vs control 28.9%, +0.7pt, p=.04. Second cohort did not reproduce; combined estimate no longer significant. Support tickets were flat — useful operational evidence, but the activation claim did not hold.

  Counter-pattern to watch: "support didn't go up, so it's safe to ship." That is the wrong risk axis. The relevant question is whether the effect reproduces.

  Decision rule: "first significant read" is a status, not a conclusion. A rollout needs a second cohort or a clean confounder read.

[18:00–23:00]  EXERCISE — BAD-TO-BETTER READOUT (5 min, room)

---

[Reply body, for Priya to forward]

Hi — thanks for raising this, and glad to hear CS found the Q4 guidance useful.

I'm comfortable making the guidance findable and reusable for any team that asks Growth for experiment or churn-read support. What I'd want to avoid this quarter is making it a required companywide template, for two specific reasons:

1. The two safeguards in the guidance — effect size travels with the hypothesis stack, and first statistical significance is not a ship decision without a stabilization cohort — only hold when the readout owner is the experiment owner. A mandated format tends to produce the exact drift the guidance is meant to prevent: clean-looking readouts that cite first significance without stabilization context, or that lead with a recommendation and bury effect size. That's the failure mode the document exists to catch, not enable.

2. A companywide mandate would also collapse two review lanes that need to stay distinct. Owen owns standard readout shape and effect-size placement, so the readout is read the way the framework intends. Ines owns lifecycle-risk language, so drift toward "launch," "funnel," "pipeline," or "not yet" framing doesn't sneak back in. Those reviews are domain-specific and only work if each reviewer stays in their lane.

What I'd propose instead:

- The guidance stays where it is in the Growth folder ("Q4 investigation readout guidance — lightweight trial") and is findable to anyone who'd ask Growth for support. Happy to add a short pointer wherever is useful.
- Any team can borrow it as a starting checklist — cohort cuts, hypothesis stack, effect size before the conclusion, first-significance vs. stabilization-cohort framing. Owen and Ines have already sanity-checked the safeguards, so they're baked in.
- Teams that want a deeper review can loop Owen in for readout shape / effect-size questions and Ines for lifecycle-risk language. They don't have to, but the lanes are open.

If the trial has been borrowed cleanly by a few teams by end of quarter, that's the read I'd use to revisit whether a broader standard makes sense later — and it would still need Owen and Ines in their lanes to work.

Happy to talk through any of this if useful before it goes wider.

Riley

---

Thanks for routing this through me. I'm fine making the doc findable; I just don't want it to turn into a Q4 mandate, since that tends to produce the very drift the safeguards exist to prevent.

arguments.body:
H2 WORK LOG — Seasonal & competitor-cycle comp

Owner: Riley
Pair-check: Owen (before any number is locked)
Status: SKELETON. Awaiting historical data pull + Owen availability.
Linked to: "Mid-seg churn spike -- Feb 2023 investigation" (parent doc).

QUESTION
Is the Jan 2023 mid_seg (50-200 seats) churn signal — 5.1% monthly vs.
2.1% trailing-six-month baseline — consistent with prior-year same-window
seasonality, or does it represent a competitor-cycle disturbance?

WHY THIS QUESTION, WHY NOW
H1 (pricing artifact) closed Feb 15 with Owen: tier split was entry 5.0%,
standard 5.2%, plus 5.1%, all within ~20 bps. Tier-agnostic pattern
argues against pricing/contract-mix as primary cause. Hypothesis weight
now tilts toward H3 (onboarding timing lag) and H4 (CS coverage) and the
remaining competitor question — H2.

The "weird Feb blip" hand-wave is exactly what this read is designed to
prevent. If Feb has historically been a noisier month for mid_seg, the
Jan signal may be a tail of seasonal churn, not a step change. If Feb
has been clean historically, the Jan signal is the real story.

METHOD (HARD RULES)
- Same-window prior-year comps. NO cherry-picked months. If a month
  gets excluded, the reason goes in this doc with a timestamp.
- Owen pulls fresh from the warehouse. NO recycled query tabs.
  Contamination risk: a saved tab from a prior cut can quietly encode
  a different segment definition or a different dedup rule.
- Every number cited in the readout must carry: tier, segment-def
  version (v1: 50-200 seats), seat-count field name, snapshot date,
  dedup rule, query timestamp, analyst.
- If I rerun, I rerun from the warehouse, not from a saved result.
- Pricing-page guardrail: this work lives in the investigation thread.
  Marcus's pricing-page experiment (design late Feb, ship first week
  Mar, ~3-week run) is a separate causal question with a different
  unit of analysis. If anyone tries to fuse the two, push back and
  re-document the separation here.

COMPARISON WINDOWS (TARGET)
Mid_seg (v1: 50-200 seats), monthly churn rate, monthly anchor:
- 2021-01, 2021-02, 2021-06, 2021-09, 2021-12
- 2022-01, 2022-02, 2022-03, 2022-06, 2022-09, 2022-12
- 2023-01 (the signal), 2023-02 (in-progress, if mid-month is callable)

Also pull mid_seg churned_accounts and churned_mrr for the same windows
so we can distinguish a rate move driven by account count vs. a rate
move driven by $-weight.

CONTRAST SET
Same series for growth and enterprise tiers over the same windows.
Purpose: if Feb is noisy company-wide, that's a seasonality story. If
Feb is noisy only in mid_seg, that's a mid_seg-specific story and
weakens the "weird Feb blip" framing in a different direction.

COMPETITOR / MARKET OVERLAY (TARGET)
- Cancel-reason text for Jan 2023 mid_seg churners. Specific asks:
  does "switching to [competitor]" or "cheaper alternative" appear in
  any non-trivial share? Does "missing feature X" cluster?
- Inbound competitor signal in the Dec-Jan window: pricing-page
  changes, public announcements, ad launches, conference presence,
  newsletters targeting our ICP.
- Known B2B SaaS seasonality markers: calendar-year budget flush
  (early Dec), fiscal-year-end cycles by customer (varies), post-
  holiday contraction (early Jan).
- Series-B date (Apr 2022) and any onboarding/contract changes since.

TIMELINE
- Feb 17 (today): skeleton + Owen ping.
- Feb 18-21 (the planned H2 window): historical pull, comps table,
  cancel-reason pass, overlay markers. Owen pair-check on the
  headline numbers.
- Feb 21 target: Owen one-pager (why, cuts, p-value/effect-size if
  applicable, call) — same shape as the H1 one-pager.
- Feb 21-22: post in #growth-investigations. Tag Priya. Marcus
  included only as a stakeholder FYI line; the pricing-page thread
  is NOT used.
- Feb 28 onward: H3 (onboarding timing lag) starts to clarify if H2
  is closed. If H2 stays open past Feb 21, escalate the framing in
  the next staff sync — not because the world is on fire, but
  because the H2 window was the planned one.

DATA-ACCESS NOTE (2023-02-17)
First pass against the metrics endpoints returned no historical
snapshots (NOT_FOUND on every probe). If the warehouse is reachable
directly, Owen's pull is the path. If neither path surfaces the
historical anchors above, H2 cannot close inside the planned window
and we say so in the readout rather than substituting vibes.

ANTI-CONTAMINATION LOG
- 2023-02-17 09:xx — Skeleton created. No queries run yet.
- (append rows as Owen and I execute)

OPEN QUESTIONS
- Confirm v1 segment definition still governs: 50-200 seats, which
  field, which dedup rule.
- Confirm the trailing-six-month baseline of 2.1% was computed over
  the same v1 definition (not a different segment version).
- Identify the cancel-reason field source: CRM tag, exit-survey
  text, support ticket, or all three.
- Identify any internal channel where competitor mentions are
  captured (sales-loss-reasons, CSM notes, win/loss interviews).

  - Inconclusive. Landed 2023-06-29; flag `expansion_nudge_60d_v1` rolled back to 0% on 2023-07-20 so lingering exposure could not be read as rollout momentum.

  - Cohort: retained mid-segment v2 accounts, 75–200 seats; prompt at day 60; metric of record was expansion MRR per account in days 60–90.
